strengths: RegCache presents a technically interesting, training-free extension of attention-sink/register ideas to activation quantization of vision encoders. Middle-layer KV prefixing combined with deletion of emerging outlier tokens is reasonably original and well motivated by the observed difference between language and vision models.

The empirical gains are often large, especially at 6-bit precision and for otherwise fragile configurations such as SigLIP2. Evaluation spans CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and DINOv2; multiple quantizers; classification and retrieval; and several transfer datasets.

The paper provides useful diagnostic evidence connecting layerwise quantization sensitivity to activation outliers. The cross-image similarity measurement, norm reductions, foreground/background analysis, and component ablation collectively support the proposed mechanism.

Compatibility experiments with FIMA-Q, QuaRot-style rotation, AWQ, and a prior test-time-register method strengthen the practical case. Reported FLOP overhead is small, and the manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate. The deletion-count search range, selected hyperparameters for every model/quantizer, precise rule for choosing among the preceding insertion blocks, quantizer granularities/scales, and implementation details of propagating or constructing layerwise KV caches are not fully reported. The method is highly configuration-dependent, including a separate DINOv2 insertion policy.

The method requires 50,000 ImageNet training images, labeled reference-task accuracy, layerwise sensitivity evaluation, and searches over prefix copies and deletion counts for each encoder/base quantizer. Thus, although gradient-free, it involves substantial task-specific calibration and validation; the paper understates this cost and does not test sensitivity to reference-set size, labels, domain shift, random seed, or hyperparameter choice.

The systems evidence is insufficient for an efficiency-motivated quantization paper. FLOPs are computed using pseudo-quantization, and latency is reported for an entire dataset without batch size, quantized kernels, precision implementation, warm-up, variance, or hardware-specific deployment details. Dynamic norm computation, top-k token deletion, and KV insertion may introduce nontrivial synchronization and memory overhead on edge hardware; the assertion that caching can easily remove the roughly 5% slowdown is unsupported.

The main ablation is limited to naive W8A8 on only SigLIP and SigLIP2. There is no controlled comparison of top-outlier averaging against random/background/centroid prefixes, no candidate-pool-size or number-of-prefix/deleted-token curves, and no ablation across the stronger quantizers. This leaves uncertainty about which design decisions are essential and how robustly they transfer.

Several inconsistencies reduce confidence in the results: Table 8 appears to swap the CLIP and OpenCLIP names relative to their known and elsewhere-reported FP32 accuracies; DINOv2 is inconsistently called B/14 and B/16; and the text claims consistent FIMA-Q improvements although every SigLIP2 classification result decreases. Some near-identical FIMA-Q values across bitwidths also merit verification.

The explanation of universality is still preliminary: cosine similarity is measured on only 64 ImageNet images, while the lemma merely formalizes that vectors sharing an increasingly dominant coordinate become similar and does not establish why the model creates aligned outlier channels. Transfer experiments show usefulness on several classification datasets, but do not evaluate stronger distribution shifts, dense prediction, larger encoder scales, or non-ImageNet calibration sources.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant practical problem: activation outliers substantially damage low-bit quantization of pretrained vision encoders. The layerwise sensitivity measurements and token-norm statistics provide useful empirical motivation.

RegCache is conceptually intuitive and training-free: it caches middle-layer register key/value vectors and deletes emerging high-norm tokens. Adapting attention-sink prefixing to vision encoders, where sinks emerge only after several blocks, is a meaningful technical contribution.

The evaluation covers five encoder families, 4/6/8-bit settings, classification and retrieval, and several PTQ baselines. Improvements are often large in difficult settings, including gains of 10–25 points over several 6-bit baselines, while cross-dataset experiments suggest some transfer beyond ImageNet.

The paper includes component ablations, norm measurements, latency/FLOP estimates, a comparison with test-time registers, and experiments with FIMA-Q and rotation-based quantization. The manuscript is generally organized and visually clear.
weaknesses: The practical efficiency case is not adequately established. Experiments primarily use pseudo/dynamic quantization, and the reported FLOPs are explicitly based on simulated quantized operations. There is no evaluation using deployed integer kernels, end-to-end throughput, memory, or energy on the edge hardware motivating the work. RegCache actually increases measured CLIP/OpenCLIP latency by about 5%, while the assertion that hardware caching can easily remove this overhead is unsupported.

Reproducibility is weak. Critical selected values are not reported per model and quantizer, including the sensitive layer, insertion layers, number of prefix copies, and number of deleted tokens. The precise construction and propagation of layer-specific averaged KV caches is underspecified, as are safeguards concerning class tokens and semantically important patches. The method also performs substantial labeled ImageNet-based selection over layers and multiple hyperparameters, complicating the characterization as a simple training-free plug-in.

The experimental isolation is incomplete. There is no full-precision-plus-RegCache control, so it is unclear how much of the change comes from altering the representation through token deletion rather than specifically reducing quantization error. The ablation evidence is limited to two models and does not convincingly support the claimed synergy: caching alone essentially matches the combined result on SigLIP, whereas deletion alone accounts for most of the gain on SigLIP2.

The mechanistic conclusions are stronger than the evidence. The foreground/background experiment is shown only for one model and is confounded by the severe distribution shift introduced by zeroing image regions. The register-versus-no-register DINO comparison involves differently trained models, so it does not establish tokenization as the cause of early outliers. The appendix lemma is a generic fact about aligned large coordinates and does not explain why those coordinates align or why cached registers mitigate them.

Originality relative to the closest work remains uncertain. The approach closely combines LLM prefix quantization with prior test-time register insertion/deletion for ViTs. The direct comparison with the latter is confined to two models, one W8A8 setting, and naive quantization, without sufficient implementation detail or comparisons under the stronger PTQ baselines where the paper's contribution is most relevant.

There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, sensitivity analyses for the tuned hyperparameters, or held-out selection results. Since the method selects configurations using ImageNet classification accuracy and many reported gains at W8A8 are below one point, selection variance and overfitting are important. Generalization experiments use only naive W8A8 quantization rather than the stronger baselines.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence: Table 8 appears to swap the CLIP and OpenCLIP full-precision accuracies relative to the main table; DINOv2 is alternately labeled B/14 and B/16; and the latency column is labeled "m/s" although its entries are total minutes and seconds. These may be correctable, but they reinforce the need for clearer experimental documentation.

strengths: The paper presents an original and practically relevant Algorithms/General contribution: RegCache adapts attention-sink prefixing to vision encoders through middle-layer insertion and token deletion, addressing a meaningful obstacle to activation quantization.

The motivating analysis is coherent and useful. Layerwise sensitivity aligns with the emergence of large activations, outlier tokens have high cross-image cosine similarity (0.89 versus 0.26 for normal tokens), and the foreground/background experiment provides evidence for why vision outliers emerge only after early visual processing.

The empirical evaluation is broad across CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and DINOv2; 4/6/8-bit settings; classification and retrieval; and several PTQ baselines. Improvements are often substantial at challenging precisions—for example, RegCache improves RepQ-ViT W6A6 ImageNet accuracy by 13.48 points on CLIP and 21.84 points on OpenCLIP.

The method is complementary to multiple quantizers, including PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, and rotation-based quantization. Tests on four non-ImageNet classification datasets also support transfer of the ImageNet-derived cache.

The ablation, token-norm measurements, insertion-layer study, comparison with test-time registers, and latency/FLOP analysis collectively provide evidence for the proposed mechanism rather than reporting accuracy gains alone.
The paper is well organized, visually clear, and appropriately relates the approach to prior work on ViT registers, attention sinks, and post-training quantization.
weaknesses: Calling RegCache training-free is technically reasonable but understates its data and tuning requirements. It searches sensitive layers and multiple hyperparameters using labeled ImageNet classification accuracy, draws candidates from 50,000 training images, and evaluates up to 15 prefix multiplicities. This is substantially more task-specific supervision and data than the 32–1,024 calibration samples used by some baselines; a data-matched comparison and results using an unlabeled or much smaller calibration set are needed.

Reproducibility is limited by missing selected hyperparameters and procedural details. The paper does not tabulate the insertion layer, number of prefix copies, or deletion count for every model/quantizer, nor clearly specify the validation subset and whether tuning is repeated independently for each precision. Sensitivity to the candidate-pool size, top-k=100 choice, and calibration seed is also absent.

The scope is narrower than the deployment motivation suggests: all evaluated encoders are base-sized, and downstream evidence is limited to global classification and retrieval. Deleting image tokens could be consequential for detection, segmentation, localization, or embodied-control tasks, so claims about broad plug-and-play applicability should be qualified or supported on dense prediction tasks.

Results are generally strong but not uniformly positive. RegCache slightly harms several DINOv2 and FIMA-Q/SigLIP2 configurations, and some 4-bit settings remain near unusable accuracy. The manuscript's repeated claims of consistent improvement should therefore be softened.

There are reporting inconsistencies that should be corrected: Table 8 appears to swap the CLIP and OpenCLIP FP32 values relative to the main table; the DINOv2 patch size is inconsistently written as B/14 and B/16; Table 12 labels latency as “m/s” although entries are elapsed minutes; and some SigLIP2 values in Table 9 appear unusually duplicated from SigLIP, warranting verification.

The systems evidence does not yet establish actual deployment benefits. CLIP and OpenCLIP become roughly 5% slower, FLOPs are estimated using pseudo-quantization, and no real integer-kernel throughput, memory, or energy measurements are provided. Thus, the accuracy contribution is convincing, but the claimed edge-efficiency benefit remains only partially demonstrated.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important activation-outlier problem in large pretrained vision encoders and proposes a sensible Algorithms/General contribution: RegCache combines middle-layer KV prefixing with deletion of newly emerging sink tokens, without updating model parameters.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad: five standalone encoders, several PTQ algorithms, 4/6/8-bit settings, classification and retrieval tasks, multiple out-of-domain datasets, and image/video VLM benchmarks. Many improvements are large, especially for otherwise fragile 4- and 6-bit configurations.

The analyses connect layerwise quantization sensitivity, outlier emergence, and cross-image similarity. Comparisons with test-time registers, component ablations, outlier-norm measurements, a label-free reconstruction criterion, and a dense-prediction adaptation provide useful support beyond headline accuracy.
The TensorRT measurements show that INT8 quantization provides meaningful speedups and that RegCache adds only about 0.01–1.54% measured latency overhead, supporting practical relevance.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript does not report the selected sensitive and prefix-start layers, prefix multiplicities, deletion counts, or other final hyperparameters for each model–quantizer pair. Implementation details for constructing and propagating the per-layer KV caches and integrating token deletion into VLMs are also underspecified, and no code-release statement is given.

The strongest claimed benefits concern 4-bit inference, but hardware latency is measured only for INT8. Most 4-bit results appear to use simulated quantization, and many non-FIMA-Q W4A4 configurations remain at very low absolute accuracy even after improvement. Thus the evidence does not establish an efficient deployable 4-bit system.

RegCache requires a substantial model- and quantizer-specific search: candidate construction uses 50,000 ImageNet training images, while sensitive-layer selection, prefix multiplicity, and deletion count are tuned using reference-task accuracy. This weakens the presentation as a lightweight universal plug-in. The label-free alternative is encouraging but is evaluated on only two encoders and still requires calibration/search.

The mechanistic conclusions are stronger than the evidence. The foreground/background masking experiment is confounded by severe input-distribution changes, and the elementary cosine-similarity lemma does not establish that outlier tokens are semantic-free universal registers. The tokenization explanation similarly compares differently trained DINOv2 variants rather than isolating tokenization causally.

Some interpretations and summary claims are inaccurate. Table 8 does not show both components acting synergistically on both encoders: prefixing alone nearly saturates the SigLIP result, while deletion alone nearly saturates SigLIP2. The claimed consistent improvement also has several small counterexamples in Tables 2–3, particularly for DINOv2 W8A8. Overall, the promising results slightly outweigh these concerns, but fuller specification and real low-bit deployment evidence are needed for a confident accept.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant problem: activation outliers make low-bit quantization of large vision encoders difficult, and the proposed RegCache module is training-free in the narrow sense of requiring no gradient-based model updates.

The middle-layer observation is interesting and reasonably motivated. The layerwise sensitivity analysis, cross-image cosine similarity of outlier tokens, and foreground/background experiment provide useful empirical evidence that vision-encoder sinks behave differently from those in language models.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering five standalone encoders, several PTQ methods, 4/6/8-bit settings, classification, retrieval, image and video VLM benchmarks, and a limited dense-prediction experiment. RegCache frequently produces substantial gains, especially where baseline low-bit quantization collapses.

Experiments on datasets beyond ImageNet and on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA offer evidence that the cached registers are not entirely tied to one downstream benchmark. The comparison with test-time registers and the reconstruction-loss selection variant are also valuable.
The reported TensorRT measurements suggest that adding RegCache to INT8 inference incurs little latency overhead, and the paper clearly presents its motivation and overall mechanism.
weaknesses: The strongest deployment claim is not adequately demonstrated. Most large accuracy gains occur at W4A4 or W6A6, but actual latency is reported only for INT8. At W8A8, improvements over strong PTQ baselines are generally small and occasionally negative. The paper therefore does not establish that its most favorable low-bit configurations yield realizable hardware speedups rather than pseudo-quantization gains.

Calling the procedure training-free obscures a substantial model- and quantizer-specific selection process: it uses 50,000 ImageNet training images, labels and classification accuracy to identify sensitive layers and tune the number of cached and deleted tokens, with repeated validation for each encoder and base PTQ method. The one-hour figure covers only a naive RTN search, not the full cost across the many reported combinations. This weakens the claimed plug-and-play practicality.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The manuscript does not tabulate the selected insertion layers, number of prefix copies, deletion counts, candidate-pool details, or complete search protocol for each model/PTQ combination. These are central algorithmic choices rather than minor implementation details, and the acknowledged heuristic per-configuration tuning makes their omission consequential.

The generalization argument is incomplete because the downstream datasets reuse prefixes selected on ImageNet, but there is no systematic analysis across different reference datasets, reference-set sizes, or domain shifts. The label-free reconstruction variant is shown only for CLIP and SigLIP, leaving unclear whether the expensive supervised selection can generally be avoided.

Token deletion changes the representation and removes spatial tokens based on each input. Its semantic risks are evaluated only through one ADE20K/SigLIP/W8A8 experiment that introduces an additional interpolation variant absent from the main method. More evidence is needed for localization, detection, segmentation, small-object recognition, and VLM tasks that may depend on the deleted patches.

Several mechanistic claims are stronger than the evidence. High cosine similarity can be a largely mechanical consequence of aligned dominant channels, as the appendix lemma itself shows; it does not establish that the tokens constitute a semantic or universal register. Likewise, the foreground/background experiment is narrow and does not rule out alternative explanations for middle-layer outlier emergence.

The ablation is limited to two models and one naive W8A8 setting. It even shows that caching or deletion individually can severely hurt performance, making the method sensitive and motivating broader component ablations, robustness curves, and uncertainty across calibration samples or random seeds.

The paper is best assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. It has enough novelty and empirical breadth for a slight acceptance preference, but the missing low-bit hardware validation, extensive hidden selection burden, and incomplete reproducibility prevent a stronger score.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important problem: activation outliers make large pretrained vision encoders difficult to quantize, even when established ViT PTQ methods are used. The proposed training-free RegCache module is technically intuitive, lightweight at inference, and complementary to multiple existing quantizers.

The central empirical observations are interesting and relevant to computer vision: vision-encoder outliers emerge mainly in intermediate layers, coincide with quantization-sensitive layers, and exhibit high cross-image similarity. These observations motivate the middle-layer prefixing and token-deletion design rather than merely transferring an LLM technique unchanged.

The experimental evaluation is unusually broad. It covers five vision encoders, classification and retrieval, multiple image datasets, dense prediction, image/video VLM benchmarks, several PTQ families, bit widths from 4 to 8, and additional weight-only, rotation-based, and SmoothQuant settings.

Results are generally compelling. RegCache produces large improvements in difficult low-bit regimes and consistent gains on VLM benchmarks. Cross-dataset evaluation supports the claim that ImageNet-curated registers can transfer beyond the reference dataset.

The paper includes useful mechanism and deployment evidence: RegCache substantially reduces maximum token norms, component ablations demonstrate complementarity, comparison with test-time registers favors the proposed curation, and TensorRT measurements show only about 0.01–1.54% latency overhead while retaining roughly 2–2.8x acceleration over full precision.

The manuscript is clearly organized, visually polished, and appropriately discusses limitations. The reconstruction-loss selection variant is also valuable because it shows that labels and downstream metrics are not fundamentally required.
weaknesses: The default procedure is less turnkey than the presentation suggests. It uses 50,000 ImageNet training images, layerwise sensitivity evaluation, candidate selection, and model-and-quantizer-specific searches over the insertion layer, prefix multiplicity, and deletion count. Although no weights are trained, this substantial calibration and hyperparameter tuning weakens the practical meaning of “training-free” and “go-to” deployment.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The paper does not clearly tabulate the selected sensitive layer, insertion range, prefix count, deletion count, and other final hyperparameters for every model and quantizer. Exact quantizer configurations and the implementation path connecting pseudo-quantized accuracy experiments to TensorRT kernels also need clearer specification.

The label-free reconstruction-loss search is demonstrated only for CLIP-B/16 and SigLIP-B/16. Broader validation is needed before concluding that RegCache remains generally practical when ImageNet labels or a representative reference task are unavailable.

The causal account of universal registers is suggestive rather than conclusive. The appendix lemma only establishes that vectors sharing a dominant coordinate have high cosine similarity; it does not explain why particular channels align across images or why the resulting cached tokens suppress other outliers. The foreground/background and registered-DINOv2 analyses support the hypothesis but do not fully establish it.

Some results reveal limited universality. DINOv2 has an average W8A8 degradation and requires a different insertion policy, while several W4A4 results remain close to unusable despite relative gains. Claims of consistent improvement should therefore be qualified by architecture, baseline, and operating regime.

The ablation evidence is narrow: caching and deletion are jointly studied on only two models, and each component alone can severely harm performance. This makes robust hyperparameter selection particularly important and motivates sensitivity analyses for the candidate-pool size, number of cached copies, number of deleted tokens, and calibration-set composition.

The efficiency evidence mainly measures INT8 deployment, whereas many headline accuracy gains occur at W4A4 or W6A6. End-to-end measurements for those low-bit regimes, including search/calibration cost and memory overhead, would better support the practical deployment claims.
